data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a 'critical rationality' decision rule that maximizes error elimination potential without assuming future uniformity.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the preference logically entails a premise that the future will resemble the past.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the concept of 'verisimilitude' cannot be defined without inductive assumptions.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If acting on the theory requires believing it is likely true.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between the logical status of corroboration (a report of past performance) and the pragmatic decision to prefer the theory that has withstood the most severe tests.
